title: System Design
blurb: From the interview framework through networking, data, messaging and distributed systems to 15 classic case studies. Do the must nodes in order, then pick cases that match your target company.
audience: Backend and full-stack engineers preparing for HLD and LLD rounds

nodes.title: The interview framework
nodes.summary: Requirements, estimates, API, data model, architecture, deep dives, trade-offs: in that order, in 45 minutes. Structure is half the score.
checklist: Split functional and non-functional requirements and confirm scope in the first 5 minutes
Ask about scale, read/write ratio, latency target and consistency needs before drawing
Sketch the API (endpoints or RPCs) and the core entities before the box diagram
Draw a high-level diagram, then pick 2-3 deep dives the interviewer cares about
Name every trade-off out loud: what you chose, what you gave up, when you would switch
Finish with bottlenecks, failure modes and how you would monitor the system

links.title: ByteByteGo: a framework for system design interviews
Hello Interview: system design delivery framework

nodes.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
nodes.summary: QPS, storage, bandwidth and the latency numbers every engineer should know. Estimates decide whether you need sharding, caching or nothing at all.
checklist: Convert daily active users into average and peak QPS (1 day is about 10^5 seconds)
Estimate storage for 5 years from object size, write rate and replication factor
Estimate bandwidth and decide whether a CDN is required
Recall rough latencies: memory read, SSD read, same-datacentre round trip, cross-continent round trip
Compute availability from nines (99.9% is about 43 minutes of downtime a month)
Use estimates to justify a decision (one Postgres box is enough, or it is not)

links.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know

nodes.title: Scaling from zero to millions
nodes.summary: Single server, then load balancer, replication, cache, CDN, stateless web tier, queues and sharding. The mental model behind every later node.
checklist: Explain why the web tier must be stateless before you can scale it horizontally
Move sessions out of process memory into a shared store or signed cookies
Add read replicas and explain what replication lag does to read-your-writes
Put a cache and a CDN in front and say which traffic each one absorbs
Decouple slow work with a queue and workers
Say when vertical scaling is still the right answer

links.title: ByteByteGo: scale from zero to millions of users

nodes.title: DNS and global routing
nodes.summary: How a name becomes an IP address, and how DNS is used for failover and geo-routing. Explains why DNS changes are slow and why TTLs matter.
checklist: Walk a lookup: stub resolver, recursive resolver, root, TLD and authoritative servers
Explain A, AAAA, CNAME, NS and TXT records
Explain TTLs and why clients and resolvers may keep stale answers after a change
Describe GeoDNS and latency-based routing for multi-region traffic
Explain anycast and why big DNS and CDN providers use it

links.title: Julia Evans: how updating DNS works
RFC 1034: domain names, concepts and facilities

nodes.title: TCP and UDP
nodes.summary: Reliable ordered streams versus fire-and-forget datagrams. Connection setup cost and head-of-line blocking shape every protocol above them.
checklist: Explain the TCP three-way handshake and what it costs in round trips
Explain flow control versus congestion control and slow start
Explain head-of-line blocking in TCP
Say when UDP is the right choice (DNS, games, voice, QUIC)
Explain why connection pooling and keep-alive matter for latency

links.title: High Performance Browser Networking: building blocks of TCP
High Performance Browser Networking: building blocks of UDP

nodes.title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
nodes.summary: What each HTTP version fixed: keep-alive, multiplexing, header compression, and QUIC over UDP. Comes up whenever you discuss latency or gateways.
checklist: Explain request/response semantics, methods, status codes and idempotent methods
Explain HTTP/2 multiplexing and why it still suffers TCP head-of-line blocking
Explain how HTTP/3 over QUIC removes that and speeds up connection setup
Explain HTTP caching headers: Cache-Control, ETag, and conditional requests
Say where HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 terminates in a typical load balancer setup

nodes.title: TLS and certificates
nodes.summary: How TLS 1.3 sets up an encrypted, authenticated connection in one round trip, and where to terminate it in your architecture.
checklist: Walk the TLS 1.3 handshake and say what is authenticated and what is encrypted
Explain certificates, chains of trust and certificate authorities
Explain TLS termination at the load balancer versus end-to-end TLS
Explain mutual TLS (mTLS) for service-to-service authentication
Explain session resumption and 0-RTT, and the replay risk of 0-RTT

nodes.title: WebSockets, SSE and long polling
nodes.summary: The options for pushing data to clients, what each costs on the server, and how to scale long-lived connections behind load balancers.
checklist: Compare short polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets
Explain why long-lived connections need sticky routing or a connection registry
Fan out messages to the right gateway node via pub/sub
Handle reconnects, heartbeats and resuming from a last-seen id
Estimate memory and file-descriptor cost per open connection

nodes.title: Load balancing
nodes.summary: L4 vs L7, algorithms, health checks, and a pluggable balancer in code. The first box you draw in almost every design.
checklist: Explain L4 versus L7 load balancing and what each can see
Compare round robin, least connections, weighted and consistent-hash routing
Design active and passive health checks and connection draining
Explain sticky sessions and why stateless services avoid them
Avoid the load balancer being a single point of failure (pairs, DNS, anycast)

nodes.title: Reverse proxy and API gateway
nodes.summary: A single front door that terminates TLS, routes, authenticates and rate-limits. Know where a gateway helps and where it becomes a bottleneck.
checklist: Explain forward proxy versus reverse proxy
List gateway responsibilities: routing, auth, rate limits, request shaping, observability
Explain the backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern
Explain why business logic should not live in the gateway
Say how the gateway itself scales and fails

nodes.title: CDN and edge caching
nodes.summary: Edge caching, TLS termination close to users and push vs pull CDNs. The cheapest way to cut latency and origin load for static and cacheable content.
checklist: Compare pull and push CDNs and when each fits
Design cache keys and Cache-Control headers for static and dynamic content
Invalidate content with versioned URLs versus purges
Explain origin shielding and how a CDN protects the origin during spikes
Say what can run at the edge (redirects, auth checks, A/B routing)

nodes.title: Caching layers
nodes.summary: Cache-aside, write strategies, eviction, stampede, invalidation and an LRU cache. Every read-heavy design leans on it.
checklist: Compare cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-back
Explain LRU, LFU and TTL eviction and implement an LRU cache
Prevent a cache stampede with request coalescing, locks or early refresh
Handle hot keys with replication or local in-process caches
Choose an invalidation strategy and explain the stale-read window
Layer caches: browser, CDN, application, database buffer pool

nodes.title: Rate limiting
nodes.summary: Token bucket, sliding window and distributed counters. Protects services from abuse and noisy neighbours.
checklist: Implement token bucket and sliding-window counter from scratch
Compare fixed window, sliding log and sliding window counter on accuracy and memory
Make a limiter atomic across many servers with Redis and a Lua script
Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers
Decide what to key on: user, API key, IP, endpoint

links.title: Stripe: scaling your API with rate limiters
Cloudflare: counting things, a lot of different things

nodes.title: API design for system design rounds
nodes.summary: REST, gRPC and GraphQL, pagination, versioning and idempotent writes. The API is the contract your whole design hangs from.
checklist: Design resource-oriented REST endpoints with correct methods and status codes
Choose between REST, gRPC and GraphQL for a given client
Use cursor pagination instead of offset for large or changing lists
Version an API without breaking existing clients
Accept idempotency keys on create and payment endpoints

nodes.title: SQL vs NoSQL and choosing a database
nodes.summary: Relational, document, key-value, wide-column, graph and time-series stores, and how to choose by access pattern instead of by fashion.
checklist: Name the data model and a typical use case for each database family
Choose a store from access patterns, consistency needs and scale
Explain why joins and transactions push you toward relational
Design a DynamoDB or Cassandra table from partition and sort keys
Explain when one Postgres instance beats a distributed database

nodes.title: Indexes and query plans
nodes.summary: How B-tree, hash, composite and covering indexes speed reads and slow writes. Most real scaling problems are a missing index.
checklist: Explain how a B+ tree index finds a row in O(log n) page reads
Apply the leftmost-prefix rule to a composite index
Use covering and partial indexes to avoid table lookups
Read an EXPLAIN plan and spot a sequential scan
Explain the write and storage cost of every extra index

nodes.title: Storage engines: LSM trees vs B-trees
nodes.summary: Why write-heavy stores like Cassandra and RocksDB use LSM trees while Postgres and MySQL use B-trees, and what that means for reads, writes and compaction.
checklist: Explain the write path of an LSM tree: WAL, memtable, SSTables, compaction
Explain how Bloom filters keep LSM point reads cheap
Compare read, write and space amplification of LSM and B-tree engines
Explain why B-trees update pages in place and need a WAL
Pick an engine for a write-heavy time-series or log workload

nodes.title: Transactions and isolation levels
nodes.summary: ACID, the anomalies each isolation level allows, and optimistic versus pessimistic locking. Needed for any design that moves money or inventory.
checklist: Explain ACID and what the database actually guarantees
Name the anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew
Map Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable to the anomalies they prevent
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a version column to prevent lost updates
Explain how MVCC lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other

nodes.title: Search indexes, OLAP and probabilistic structures
nodes.summary: Inverted indexes for search, column stores for analytics, and Bloom filters, HyperLogLog and Count-Min Sketch for counting at scale.
checklist: Explain an inverted index and how Elasticsearch shards and replicates it
Keep a search index in sync with the source database via CDC or events
Compare OLTP and OLAP and explain why column stores scan fast
Use a Bloom filter to skip lookups and state its false-positive trade-off
Count unique visitors with HyperLogLog and top-K with Count-Min Sketch

nodes.title: Blob and object storage
nodes.summary: Storing large files in S3-style object stores with metadata in a database, presigned URLs and multipart upload. Used by every media or file case.
checklist: Split metadata (database) from bytes (object store) and explain why
Let clients upload and download directly with presigned URLs
Use multipart upload for large files and resume after failure
Explain durability through replication and erasure coding
Serve objects through a CDN and set lifecycle rules for cold data

links.title: Amazon S3: sharing objects with presigned URLs
Werner Vogels: building and operating a pretty big storage system (S3)

nodes.title: Replication and quorums
nodes.summary: Leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless, lag and R + W > N. How data survives machine loss and serves more reads.
checklist: Compare leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication
Compare synchronous and asynchronous replication on durability and latency
Explain replication lag and fix read-your-writes and monotonic reads
Explain quorums (R + W > N) and what they do and do not guarantee
Describe failover and the split-brain risk
Resolve write conflicts: last-write-wins, version vectors, CRDTs

links.title: PostgreSQL docs: high availability and replication

nodes.title: Partitioning and sharding
nodes.summary: Range vs hash partitioning, shard keys, hot partitions and rebalancing. What you do when one machine cannot hold the data or the writes.
checklist: Compare range, hash and directory-based partitioning
Choose a shard key from the query patterns and explain the cost of a bad one
Handle hot partitions (celebrity keys) with salting or splitting
Rebalance without downtime and explain why hash mod N is a trap
Handle cross-shard queries and secondary indexes (local vs global)

links.title: Citus: principles of sharding for relational databases

nodes.title: Consistent hashing
nodes.summary: Mapping keys to nodes so that adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys. Used by caches, Dynamo-style stores and load balancers.
checklist: Explain why hash(key) mod N reshuffles almost every key when N changes
Implement a hash ring with binary search over sorted node positions
Use virtual nodes to even out load and handle heterogeneous machines
Explain consistent hashing with bounded loads
Compare with rendezvous hashing and jump consistent hash

links.title: Dynamo: Amazon's highly available key-value store (paper)
A fast, minimal memory, consistent hash algorithm (jump hash)
Google Research: consistent hashing with bounded loads

nodes.title: CAP and PACELC
nodes.summary: What you give up during a network partition, and the latency-versus-consistency trade-off the rest of the time.
checklist: State CAP precisely: during a partition, choose consistency or availability
Explain PACELC: else, choose latency or consistency
Classify real systems carefully instead of labelling them CP or AP
Pick consistency per operation (payments strong, likes eventual)

links.title: Abadi: consistency trade-offs in modern distributed databases (PACELC)
Kleppmann: please stop calling databases CP or AP

nodes.title: Consistency models
nodes.summary: Linearizable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency, and session guarantees. The vocabulary for saying exactly what a read can return.
checklist: Define linearizability with a concrete read/write timeline
Distinguish linearizability from serializability
Explain causal consistency and why it is the strongest that stays available
Explain session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, writes-follow-reads
Explain what eventual consistency promises and what it does not

nodes.title: Distributed transactions and 2PC
nodes.summary: Two-phase commit, why the coordinator is a liability, and how databases like Spanner and CockroachDB make cross-shard transactions work.
checklist: Walk two-phase commit and the blocking problem when the coordinator dies
Explain why microservices usually prefer sagas over 2PC
Explain how a distributed SQL database commits across ranges
Decide when a single-database transaction is enough

links.title: Patterns of distributed systems: two-phase commit

nodes.title: Queues, logs and Kafka
nodes.summary: Queues vs streams, consumer groups, delivery semantics, DLQs and back-pressure. The backbone of decoupled, spiky workloads.
checklist: Compare a work queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) with a replayable log (Kafka)
Explain Kafka partitions, offsets, consumer groups and ordering per partition
Compare at-most-once, at-least-once and effectively-once delivery
Use retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue for poison messages
Apply back-pressure when consumers fall behind
Choose a partition key that keeps related events ordered

nodes.title: Pub/sub and fan-out
nodes.summary: One event, many independent subscribers. How notifications, feeds and cache invalidation spread changes without coupling services.
checklist: Compare point-to-point queues with publish/subscribe topics
Fan out one event to several queues (topic plus per-consumer queue)
Explain fire-and-forget pub/sub (Redis) versus durable pub/sub (Kafka, Pub/Sub)
Handle slow subscribers without blocking fast ones

nodes.title: Idempotency and exactly-once
nodes.summary: Retries are inevitable; make them safe with idempotency keys, dedup tables and idempotent consumers.
checklist: Explain why exactly-once delivery is really at-least-once plus idempotent processing
Implement an idempotency key store with request hash and saved response
Make a consumer idempotent with a processed-message table or natural keys
Handle the race of two concurrent requests with the same key
Choose how long to keep idempotency keys

links.title: Brandur: implementing Stripe-like idempotency keys in Postgres
AWS Builders' Library: making retries safe with idempotent APIs

nodes.title: Transactional outbox and CDC
nodes.summary: Write the business row and the event in one transaction, then publish from the outbox or the database log. Fixes the dual-write problem.
checklist: Explain the dual-write problem when you update a DB and publish an event separately
Implement an outbox table and a relay that publishes and marks rows
Use change data capture (Debezium) to stream the outbox or tables
Explain ordering and duplicate delivery from the relay

nodes.title: Sagas and long-running workflows
nodes.summary: A business transaction split into local steps with compensations. How you keep order, payment and inventory services consistent without 2PC.
checklist: Model a saga as local transactions plus compensating actions
Compare choreography (events) with orchestration (a coordinator)
Handle a compensation that itself fails
Use a durable workflow engine (Temporal) for long-running sagas

nodes.title: Background jobs and distributed scheduling
nodes.summary: Running delayed, recurring and retried work reliably across many machines without running a job twice or never.
checklist: Design a job table with status, run_at, attempts and a lease
Claim jobs safely with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a lease
Retry with backoff and cap attempts before a dead-letter state
Run cron at scale without duplicate runs (leader or lease per schedule)
Make job handlers idempotent

links.title: Slack: executing cron scripts reliably at scale

nodes.title: Consensus and Raft
nodes.summary: Leader election and replicated logs. The machinery inside etcd, ZooKeeper and distributed SQL that makes a cluster agree.
checklist: Explain what consensus solves and why it needs a majority
Walk Raft leader election with terms and randomised timeouts
Walk log replication and the commit rule
Explain why a 5-node cluster tolerates 2 failures
Say where you use consensus in a design (metadata, config, locks) and where you do not

nodes.title: Leader election and leases
nodes.summary: Picking one node to do singleton work, and fencing the old leader when it comes back. Simple to draw, easy to get wrong.
checklist: Elect a leader with etcd, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes leases
Explain lease expiry and clock assumptions
Use fencing tokens so a paused old leader cannot corrupt state
Decide whether you need a leader at all (idempotent work may not)

nodes.title: Distributed locks
nodes.summary: Mutual exclusion across machines with Redis, etcd or a database, and why a lock without fencing is only a hint.
checklist: Implement a Redis lock with SET NX PX and a random token
Explain the Redlock debate and its timing assumptions
Use fencing tokens checked by the storage layer
Prefer database constraints or optimistic concurrency when they suffice

links.title: Kleppmann: how to do distributed locking

nodes.title: Time, clocks and ordering
nodes.summary: Why wall clocks lie, and how Lamport clocks, vector clocks and hybrid logical clocks order events across machines.
checklist: Explain clock skew and why timestamps cannot order events across machines
Implement a Lamport clock and say what it guarantees
Explain vector clocks and how they detect concurrent writes
Explain hybrid logical clocks and where CockroachDB uses them

Patterns of distributed systems: Lamport clock

nodes.title: Gossip and failure detection
nodes.summary: How peers in Cassandra-style clusters spread membership and detect dead nodes without a central coordinator.
checklist: Explain gossip dissemination and why it converges in O(log n) rounds
Explain heartbeat versus phi-accrual failure detection
Explain SWIM-style probing and suspicion
Explain hinted handoff, read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy

nodes.title: Timeouts, retries and load shedding
nodes.summary: Backoff with jitter, hedging, load shedding and graceful degradation. What keeps one slow dependency from taking down everything.
checklist: Set timeouts on every network call from a latency budget
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and cap total retries
Explain retry storms and use retry budgets
Shed load early with admission control and prioritise critical traffic
Explain hedged requests and tail latency at scale

AWS Builders' Library: using load shedding to avoid overload
The tail at scale (Dean and Barroso)

nodes.title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads and degradation
nodes.summary: Patterns that contain failure: stop calling a broken dependency, isolate resource pools and serve a reduced experience instead of an error.
checklist: Explain circuit breaker states: closed, open, half-open
Isolate thread or connection pools per dependency (bulkheads)

Explain cascading failures and how they start

nodes.title: Observability: logs, metrics and traces
nodes.summary: Knowing what your system is doing from the outside. Interviewers expect you to say how you would detect and debug problems in your design.
checklist: Explain what logs, metrics and traces are each good at

Add the key dashboards and alerts to your design

nodes.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
nodes.summary: Turning "reliable" into numbers you can alert on and trade against feature velocity.
checklist: Define an SLI as good events over valid events
Set an SLO and compute its error budget
Alert on burn rate instead of raw thresholds

Compute composite availability of serial and redundant components

nodes.title: Multi-region and high availability
nodes.summary: Active-passive vs active-active across zones and regions, data placement and static stability. The senior-level follow-up to almost every design.

nodes.title: Backups and disaster recovery

Protect backups from the same failure (and the same credentials) as production

nodes.title: Deployments: blue-green, canary and flags

checklist: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments
Gate a canary on SLO metrics and roll back automatically
Decouple deploy from release with feature flags

nodes.title: Authentication and authorization

Store and rotate secrets in a secrets manager

nodes.title: Monolith vs microservices

Draw service boundaries around business capabilities
Give each service its own data and explain why shared databases hurt
Explain service discovery and client- versus server-side load balancing
Say when you would not split a system

nodes.title: Event-driven architecture

checklist: Distinguish event notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing
Compare choreography with orchestration

Trace a request through asynchronous hops

nodes.title: CQRS and event sourcing

checklist: Explain CQRS and build a read model from write-side events

nodes.title: Service mesh internals
